title: The 3 high-probability setups my bot trades (real results, wins and losses)

slides.title: The 3 setups my trading bot takes
slides.caption: Real Nasdaq setups taken by our system's rules. Wins and losses.
slides.say: These are the three setups my trading bot takes using our system. Every chart in this video is a real setup on the Nasdaq, taken by our system's rules. And I'm going to show you the losses too, because that's where most traders get it wrong.

slides.title: Our system, tested trade by trade
slides.caption: trades in 19 months of real Nasdaq data · only 1 in 5 won · still up +30.7R
slides.say: We ran our system through nineteen months of real Nasdaq data, trade by trade. About three hundred trades. Only one in five of them won. And it still finished up more than thirty R. Let me show you how that's possible.

slides.title: Why 1 win in 5 is enough
points: Losses are capped at the stop | Winners run to the target
slides.say: Here's the math. The losses were capped at one R, every single time. The winners averaged more than three R. So one good trade pays for three losers. You don't need to be right often. You need your winners to be bigger than your losers.

slides.title: The idea behind all three setups
points: Find where the stops are sitting
Enter when the move fails, stop just past the wick
Target the next pool of stops
slides.say: All three setups come from one idea. Find where everyone's stops are sitting. Let the market run them. Enter when that move fails, with your stop just past the wick. And target the next pool of stops on the other side.

slides.title: Setup 1: The Opening Sweep
slides.caption: The first move of the session is often a trap.
slides.say: Setup one. The opening sweep. The first big move of the session is very often a trap.

slides.title: Opening Sweep · short · +6.7R
slides.say: July twenty seventh. Price pushed up into the open, took the stops above, and failed. Our system shorted with an eighteen point stop. Ten minutes later it hit the target. Plus six point seven R.

slides.title: Opening Sweep · long · +12.5R
slides.say: June first. Same idea, the other direction. The sell-off at the open ran the stops below, then reversed. A twelve point stop, held all day to the target. Plus twelve point five R.

slides.title: Opening Sweep · short · +11.5R
slides.say: March thirteenth. The open squeezed up, failed, and our system shorted it. A sixteen point stop, and it rode all the way down. Plus eleven point five R. Three trades, more than thirty R.

slides.title: Setup 2: The Rejection Zone
slides.caption: Price comes back to where it was rejected before.
slides.say: Setup two. The rejection zone. Price comes back to a level where it was rejected hard before, and gets rejected again.

slides.title: Rejection Zone · short · +5.7R
slides.say: November fourth. Price ran back into the zone, rejected, and our system was in with a six point stop. Plus five point seven R in six minutes.

slides.title: Rejection Zone · long · +4.2R
slides.say: September twenty second. Same zone, from below. A seven and a half point stop, target hit eight minutes later. Plus four point two R.

slides.title: Setup 3: The Second Chance
slides.caption: When your stop gets hunted, the trade isn't always over.
slides.say: Setup three. The second chance. Sometimes the market hunts your stop, and the trade still works. Here's what our system does about that.

slides.title: First entry: stopped out · −1R
slides.say: November twenty fifth. The first entry got stopped out. Minus one R. Most people quit right here.

slides.title: Second chance · +5.8R to target
slides.say: But look what happened. Price wicked through the stops and closed straight back above the entry. That's the second chance. Re-enter with a new stop past that wick, same target. Price ran all the way to the target. Held there, that's plus five point eight R.

slides.title: And this is a normal loss
slides.say: And this is what a normal loss looks like. November sixteenth. The setup was there, it didn't work, the stop got hit. Minus one R, and on to the next one. This is part of it, and it's why the risk has to be the same every time.

slides.title: The rules that keep it alive
points: The stop goes where the idea is wrong, and never moves further away
Two losses in a day and you're done
No trade unless every condition is there
slides.say: These are the rules that keep it alive. Same risk on every trade. The stop goes where the idea is wrong, and it never moves further away. Two losses in a day and you're done. And no trade unless every condition is there.

slides.title: It's not just the Nasdaq
points: Works on any chart with real volume: futures, crypto, stocks, gold
The market changes. Where the stops sit doesn't.
slides.say: And this isn't just the Nasdaq. You can use the same idea on anything with a market cap and real volume. Futures, crypto, stocks, gold. Markets change, but where the stops are sitting doesn't.
